questions.question: What is a natural hazard?
choices: Any outdoor activity regardless of danger
Only a process caused by humans
A measurement of population size
A natural process capable of causing harm

questions.question: What is exposure in hazard assessment?
choices: Presence of people or assets where a hazard may occur
Weakness of structures when affected
Probability that an event will occur
The total energy released by the event

questions.question: What is vulnerability?
choices: Presence of buildings in the affected area
Susceptibility to harm when exposed to a hazard
Probability of the hazard occurring
The strength of the event alone

questions.question: What commonly triggers a tsunami?
choices: The ordinary rise and fall of daily tides
A steady breeze across a lake
Sudden displacement of a large volume of water
Slow evaporation from the ocean

questions.question: What is a landslide?
choices: Upward growth of a mountain by plants
Formation of sea ice
Movement of air around a high-pressure center
Downslope movement of rock, soil, or debris

questions.question: What is storm surge?
choices: A storm-driven rise of seawater above the predicted tide
A sudden decrease in ocean salinity only
An underground river's normal flow
The maximum height of every wave

questions.question: What is hazard mitigation?
choices: A guarantee that no natural event can occur
Action that reduces potential harm from a hazard
Prediction of every event's exact time
Replacement of evidence with guesswork

questions.question: Why can the same earthquake cause different damage in two communities?
choices: Its magnitude changes separately for each street
Earthquakes exert no force on buildings
Exposure, construction, and ground conditions can differ
Every community has identical vulnerability

questions.question: Why can heavy rainfall increase landslide likelihood on some slopes?
choices: Rain always glues every slope securely
Water eliminates gravity
Rain prevents any soil movement
Water can add weight and reduce soil strength

questions.question: Why can paving a large area increase nearby flash-flood risk?
choices: Less infiltration can produce faster surface runoff
Pavement increases infiltration everywhere
Paving always slows runoff regardless of slope
Pavement changes rainfall into groundwater immediately

questions.question: Why is a hazard map useful even without an exact prediction?
choices: It prevents all hazards physically
It identifies areas with differing potential exposure
It gives every event's exact date
It shows that all locations are equally safe

questions.question: How do preparedness and emergency response differ?
choices: Preparedness predicts exact events; response prevents all future events
Both occur only after every danger ends
Preparedness plans before an event; response acts during or after it
Response is only a long-term rock study

questions.question: Why do warning systems not eliminate all hazard risk?
choices: A warning guarantees unlimited time to evacuate
Knowing a hazard eliminates structural vulnerability
All exposed people automatically receive and act on every warning
People still need time, access, and effective ways to act

questions.question: What is a lahar associated with a volcano?
choices: A flowing mixture of water and volcanic debris
A cloud containing only harmless steam
A slow rise in ordinary daily tides
A solid iron meteorite

questions.question: Why can drought increase wildfire risk in some landscapes?
choices: Drought increases moisture in dead vegetation
Dry vegetation can ignite and burn more readily
Dry fuels are always less likely to ignite
Fuel moisture has no influence on fire behavior

questions.question: Two towns face similar flood probability, but one has many homes on the floodplain. Which risk factor is greater there?
choices: Vulnerability of each building
Magnitude of the river's flow by definition
Exposure
Probability of the flood by definition

questions.question: A building upgrade makes structures better able to withstand expected shaking. Which risk factor is directly reduced?
choices: Earthquake magnitude
Tectonic plate speed
The depth of every future earthquake
Vulnerability

questions.question: A hazard occurs in an uninhabited region with no assets affected. Why may its losses be lower than a smaller event in a city?
choices: Exposure is much lower
Natural events cannot release energy without people nearby
The smaller city event must have more physical energy
Event size alone determines all losses

questions.question: A warning reaches residents but accessible evacuation routes are absent. What does this show?
choices: Warnings alone always eliminate structural damage
Warnings need practical response capacity to reduce harm
Evacuation routes have no relation to response options
Only the hazard's magnitude affects people's ability to act

questions.question: Records show floods of varying sizes over many decades. What use of these data is appropriate?
choices: Name the exact minute of the next flood
Conclude that past floods cannot recur
Estimate patterns and probabilities while acknowledging uncertainty
Assume every future flood will match the largest recorded event
